# Hardware-Assisted Projection

Also called: Hardware-Accelerated Cell Projection, Texture-Mapped Volume Rendering

## Overview
Hardware-Assisted Projection is a family of volume rendering techniques that project 3D volumetric cells (tetrahedra, polyhedra, or hexahedra) onto the 2D image plane, converting the volume integration problem into a series of hardware-accelerated polygon rasterization and compositing operations [S1, book]. It solves the performance bottleneck of software-based raycasting by leveraging the graphics pipeline's interpolation and blending units, trading the need for global back-to-front sorting (in standard alpha compositing variants) or complex data structures for efficient screen-space processing [S1, book]. Unlike pure raycasting, it relies on the assumption that optical properties vary linearly or can be approximated within projected regions, and unlike sorting-free additive methods, it supports arbitrary transfer functions via pre-integration textures [S1, book].

## Shared principles
All methods in this family share the core mechanism of projecting 3D geometry to 2D screen space and using hardware rasterization to compute per-pixel values [S1, book].

1.  **Projection**: 3D cell vertices are transformed into screen coordinates. The cell's projection defines the region of the image affected by that cell [S1, book].
2.  **Attribute Interpolation**: Geometric attributes (such as entry/exit scalar values, path length $l$, or attenuation) are computed at the vertices of the projected primitives and interpolated across the screen-space fragments by the hardware rasterizer [S1, book].
3.  **Hardware Compositing**: The interpolated attributes are used in the fragment shader (or fragment program) to compute color and opacity, which are then composited into the final image using hardware blending operations (typically Porter-Duff "over" for alpha compositing, or addition for absorption-only) [S1, book].
4.  **Sorting Requirement**: Standard alpha compositing requires the cells to be sorted in back-to-front order relative to the viewpoint to ensure correct transparency blending [S1, book]. Sorting-free variants exist only for specific physical models (e.g., absorption-only radiography) where the integration operator is commutative [S1, book].

### Pre-sorted Tetrahedral Rendering
This variant, introduced by Stein et al., sorts the cells before they are split into tetrahedra [S1, book]. It utilizes 2D texture mapping hardware to accelerate opacity interpolation, providing correct per-pixel opacity values to avoid artifacts [S1, book]. A key limitation is that it can only handle linear transfer functions without artifacts [S1, book].

## Background
The concept of hardware-assisted projection for volume rendering emerged in the late 1990s as graphics hardware capabilities expanded. Stein et al. [312] (cited in [S1, book]) were among the early adopters, sorting cells and using 2D texture mapping to handle opacity. Röttger et al. [272] (cited in [S1, book]) later introduced pre-integrated volume rendering, using a 3D texture map (approximated as 2D) to support arbitrary transfer functions by storing pre-computed integrals along the ray segment between cell entry and exit points [S1, book]. These methods shifted the computational burden from the CPU to the GPU's rasterization and texture units, enabling real-time visualization of unstructured grids.
